subject: Patrick
method: One writer, research and writing together (SAINT-BRIEF.md). Every quotation is in patrick.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Patrick's own words are quoted only from Newport J. D. White, St. Patrick, His Writings and Life (SPCK, 1920), public domain. The text is sources/people/patrick/white1920.clean.txt, made by clean-white.py (same folder) from the Toronto scan's OCR (archive.org stpatrick00patr, white1920b.txt): page headers, page numbers, footnote lines and footnote marks removed, line-end hyphens joined, the printer's space before a stop closed, italic I read as '/' or '1' restored, '0 Lord' read as 'O Lord'. Every White quotation was then checked letter for letter against the independent Google scan (white1920.txt, archive.org StPatrick1920); the ten that differ differ only by page breaks, footnote marks or OCR noise in the Google scan, each read by eye. Bieler's 1953 translation and the CCEL/Robot Wisdom translation were not used for any quotation. The Annals of Ulster are cited, not quoted (the CELT translation of 1983 is in copyright).

life.text: Patrick calls himself 'Patrick the sinner'; his father Calpurnius a deacon, son of Potitus a presbyter, of the village of Banavem Taberniae; a small farm nearby where he was taken; about sixteen; 'I knew not the true God'; taken to Ireland 'with many thousands of persons'.
His father was a decurion; 'I was freeborn according to the flesh'; he sold his noble rank for others; compassion toward the nation that took him captive and ruined his father's house.
life.source: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus 10, tr. White

life.text: His schooling interrupted by captivity; speech 'translated into a tongue not my own'; he blushes at his lack of education.
Tending flocks daily; a hundred prayers a day and nearly as many at night; in the woods and on the mountain; before daybreak in snow, frost, rain.
Tradition unanimously identifies the mountain with Slemish, Co. Antrim; Bury argued for Connaught; White kept Slemish.

Voices: 'Thou fastest to good purpose...'; 'Lo, thy ship is ready'; ship perhaps two hundred miles away; left the man he served six years; the ship sailed the day he arrived; the shipmaster refused, then called him back.

Three days at sea; twenty-eight days through a desert; the shipmaster's taunt; a herd of swine; wild honey 'offered in sacrifice' refused; Satan fell on him like a huge rock; he called on 'Helias' and the sun rose on him.
White's note: Helias can only mean Elijah (as Muirchú and the Lives take it), but by the time he wrote Patrick connected it with Helios, the sun.
A second captivity of two months, freed on the sixtieth night.

In Britain with his kindred who begged him not to leave; the dream of Victoricus with countless letters, 'The Voice of the Irish'; the people by the Wood of Foclut 'nigh unto the western sea' crying 'We beseech thee, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more'; 'exceedingly broken in heart'.

Charges: elders urged his sins against his episcopate; after thirty years they raised a matter he had confessed before he was a deacon, done 'in one hour' when perhaps fifteen, told to his dearest friend; that friend had said 'Lo, thou art to be raised to the rank of bishop' and later shamed him publicly.
White suggests the dearest friend may have been Germanus and the attack in Britain about 447; dates the Victoricus dream about 414-415 after Bury; Confession probably written not earlier than 454.
Elders and kin opposed his mission: gifts 'with weeping and tears'; 'Why does this fellow thrust himself into danger...'; he longed to see Britain and Gaul but was 'bound in the Spirit'.

Baptized many thousands; clergy ordained everywhere; went where none had baptized; gave presents to kings and hire to their sons; seized, bound in irons, freed on the fourteenth day; paid judges not less than the price of fifteen men; returned women's ornaments laid on the altar; the price of a shoe.
Sons and daughters of Scottic chieftains became monks and virgins of Christ; a noble lady baptized, who six days later became a virgin of Christ; slave women suffer most.
Twelve perils; daily expects slaughter, fraud, slavery; 'none of these things move me'; prays to shed his blood with the captives; the true sun, Christ; 'And this is my confession before I die.'

The Letter: soldiers of Coroticus killed the newly baptized the day after their anointing; a presbyter sent to ask for the captives; 'They jeered at them.'; 'fellow-citizens of demons'; Christians must not eat with them; the Roman Gauls ransom captives from the Franks; to be read before Coroticus himself.
Coroticus identified by White (after Ferguson, Zimmer, Bury) with Ceretic of Strathclyde, capital Alcluith, the Rock of Dumbarton; Bury conjectured the raid about 459.

Palladius sent by Celestine in 431 'to the Scots that believed in Christ, to be their first bishop' (Bede after Prosper). Sellar notes Bede mentions Patrick only in the Martyrology, not in the History.
life.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.13, tr. Sellar (1907), with note 80

life.text: Bede: 'No reptiles are found there, and no snake can live there' (of Ireland), with no mention of Patrick.

White dates Patrick 389-461 after Bury; Muirchú's first book before 699; Tírechán dated by Bury 664-668; Tírechán says Patrick spent years at Lérins (Aralanensis); Muirchú puts him with Germanus at Auxerre.
life.source: White, introduction and introduction to Muirchú

life.text: The Annals of Ulster: 431 Palladius sent; 457 'Repose of the elder Patrick, as some books state'; 461 'Here some record the repose of Patrick'; 492 the Irish state Patrick died; 493 Patrick rested on the 16th of the Kalends of April in the 120th year of his age, 60 years after coming to Ireland; 553 Colum Cille placed his relics in a shrine sixty years after his death.
life.source: The Annals of Ulster, CELT translation (Mac Airt and Mac Niocaill, 1983), cited not quoted

life.text: Catholic Encyclopedia: born Kilpatrick near Dumbarton 387, died at Saul 17 March 493; mother Conchessa 'a near relative' of Martin of Tours; in some ancient martyrologies honoured as a martyr; Brigid's shroud; Confessio and Epistola genuine; the Lorica 'now universally accepted as genuine'.

Britannica 1911 (Quiggin): born about 389; Bannauenta, possibly near the Severn; Paschal fire on the hill of Slane 'in picturesque fashion'; Saul from saball, barn; Benignus succeeded at Armagh; died 461; Muirchú's narrative in Ireland 'full of the mythical element'; Zimmer identified Palladius with Patrick; the Lorica may very well be genuine.
DNB (Olden, 1895): 493 rests on sixty years' labour from 432; burial places Saul, Downpatrick, Armagh, Glastonbury; the two Patricks; 'Chief Apostle of Ireland'; never canonised at Rome.
life.source: Dictionary of National Biography vol. 44 (1895), via Wikisource

life.text: Britannica (current): letter to Coroticus written between 451 and 496 (Franks still heathen); Palladius 431; Binchy's line on his 'rustic' Latin; 12th-century hagiography claims 33 raised; scientists say Ireland has never had snakes.
OCA: commemorated 17 March as Bishop of Armagh, Enlightener of Ireland; died 17 March 461 (some say 492); shamrock told as fact; snakes 'no historical basis'; granite slab at Downpatrick 1899.
life.source: OCA, Lives of the Saints, 17 March

later_lives.text: Muirchú: also called Sochet, of the British race; mother Concessa; Victoricus an angel; Palladius failed and died in Britain; consecration; the druids' Adze-head prophecy; Miliucc burns himself; Dichu first convert (Patrick's Barn); the Paschal fire at the Graves of the Men of Fecc seen from Tara; eight stags and a fawn; snow, darkness, trial by fire; Loiguire: 'It is better for me to believe than to die'; Daire, the bronze pot, 'Grazacham', Armagh; the hind and fawn; Coroticus turned into a fox; the hundred signs of the cross; the angel sends him back to Saul; Tassach; 17 March, 120 years; twelve nights without dark; the oxen; the war over the body; the 'fortunate delusion'.
later_lives.source: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, preface, Books 1 and 2, tr. White (1920)

later_lives.text: White's notes: grazacham = gratias agamus; Deo gratias a favourite expression; Adze-head refers to the monks' tonsure; Cothraige the Irish form of Patricius, Tírechán's 'slave in the houses of four magicians'; Historia Brittonum's four points like Moses including 120 years; 'It is plain that he died at Saul'; the Irish are Hiberionaces and Ireland Hiberio in his Latin.

Jocelin (Furness, late 1100s; for Archbishop Thomas of Armagh, Bishop Malachy of Down and John de Courcy): the threefold plague; the poisonous creatures driven from Cruachan-ailge (Croagh Patrick) into the ocean; 350 bishops, 700 churches, 5,000 priests; thirty-three dead raised.
later_lives.source: Jocelin, chapters 169, 170, 172, 185, 186 and the proeme, tr. Edmund L. Swift (1809), in O'Leary via Wikisource; O'Leary's preface for the twelfth century and Swift's 1809 Dublin printing

later_lives.text: The Lorica: preserved in the Irish Liber Hymnorum (11th century) and others; the Irish preface 'Patrick made this hymn...' (Atkinson tr.); Book of Armagh note: 'Canticum eius Scotticum semper canere'; White: no reason to deny his authorship; Atkinson on its uncouth grammar; Muirchú tells the deer story without the hymn; the name Faeth Fiada perhaps a false derivation in later times; Petrie 1839 on bedtime use; Eleanor Hull's doubt.
Episcopal Church: the Lorica 'was probably not written by him, dating most probably from the eighth century rather than from the fifth, but it does express his faith and zeal'.
C. F. Alexander's 'I bind unto myself today', source 'Writings of St. Patrick, 1889'.

myths.text: Shamrock: Threlkeld's Synopsis Stirpium Hibernicarum (first printed Dublin 1726) is the first written link of the shamrock and the Trinity; quoted from the 1727 printing on archive.org (long s normalised by NFKC).
myths.source: Threlkeld 1727 printing; The Spectator ('The first written association...', 'impossible to date', 'could indeed be founded on reality')

myths.text: Blue: earliest depictions in blue; Order of St Patrick's official colour sky blue, 'St. Patrick's Blue'; green as identity and rebellion from the late 18th century.
Birthday: the 1916 Martyrology's 'birthday' is 'the day on which a Saint enters heaven'.

feasts.text: Roman Martyrology 1916, 17 March: 'In Ireland, the birthday of St. Patrick, bishop and confessor, who was the first to preach Christ in that country...'

Calendarium Romanum 1969: 17 S. Patricii, episcopi; his depositio on 17 March (461) is recorded by several manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology and by Bede's Martyrology; added to the Roman calendar in 1631.
USCCB 2026: 17 March [Saint Patrick, Bishop], optional memorial, falling on a Lenten weekday.
Solemnity in Ireland and Australia; feast in NZ, Scotland, Wales; optional memorial in the general calendar.

Church of England: 17 Patrick, Bishop, Missionary, Patron of Ireland, c.460, printed as a Lesser Festival (no trailing italic marker, like Polycarp and Perpetua; commemorations such as Cyril of Jerusalem are marked).
Episcopal Church: 17 Patrick of Ireland, Bishop and Missionary, 461.
Lutheran: LCMS 17 March, Patrick, Missionary to Ireland (died around 466); ELCA 17 Patrick, bishop, missionary to Ireland, 461.
OCA: Saint Patrick, Bishop of Armagh, Enlightener of Ireland, 17 March. Old-calendar churches keep it on 30 March civil.

could_not_verify: Church of Ireland calendar (17 March as a festival): its site sits behind a Cloudflare check and could not be fetched, so the page does not name the Church of Ireland.
The Russian Orthodox Church's addition of Patrick to its calendar: not checked, not claimed; the page says 'the Orthodox churches that keep him'.
T. F. O'Rahilly's 'Two Patricks' (1942) is in copyright and was not read; the page gives the two-Patrick question in Olden's (1895) and the Annals' terms only.
The exact manuscript of the Montbaston miniature: Commons says 1348 and the BnF, not the shelfmark; the page says only 'a French manuscript of 1348'.
Whether Rivière meant Muirchú's fawn at Armagh: the painting matches the story, and the caption says only that it matches.
Tiepolo's date 1746 rests on Commons and Wikidata only (the Padua museum's own page returned an error).

checker_2026_09_26.checked: Every number tile (16, 6, 100 a day, 200 miles) against White's Confession. Feasts in the calendar texts on disk (Calendarium Romanum 1969 note on the Hieronymian and Bede martyrologies and 1631; USCCB; Common Worship, printed as a Lesser Festival; LFF 2022; LSB; ELCA; 1916 Martyrology) and the OCA page. Every 'X said' in context (Muirchú; the Martyrology; O'Leary's doubt, which is about the Confession and the Letter; Olden; Quiggin; White; Binchy in Britannica). The myths (Bede on snakes, Jocelin ch 170, Threlkeld via The Spectator, Smithsonian on blue and George III, the Martyrology's 'birthday', Muirchú and the Historia Brittonum on 120 years). Muirchú's burial (Dun-Lethglaisse), the twelve nights, Coroticus as a fox, Nebuchadrezzar and Babylon, the adze-head note. Short quoted phrases the script skips (under three words) checked by hand. Capitals for God; no section marks; italics (dry run: nothing); seo lengths; licences re-read on Commons (Tiepolo, Rivière PD; Clarke and Montbaston photographs CC0); the band's phone crop and the card looked at.
changed: Circle, Martin of Tours: the page said 'Olden noted Martin died too early to teach him'. Olden says the reverse: the Germanus link is the anachronism, and 'Martin of Tours without doubt was the master under whom Patrick studied'. Rewritten with his words (new evidence entry), that later Lives send Patrick to Tours, that Patrick never names Martin, and that on Bury's dates Martin died when Patrick was about eight.
Moment, Chieftains' daughters: the noble woman came back 'after a few days' and took the veil 'six days after' (Confession 42); the page had folded the two into 'came back six days later'.
The Annals of Ulster: the page quoted 'some record' and 'elder Patrick' from the CELT translation (1983, in copyright). Both now told without quotation marks, as the writer intended.

Miracles lede: 'the Lives written two centuries later' included Jocelin (late 1100s), and called Tírechán's notes a Life while other sections call Muirchú's the oldest Life. Now 'the writers who came after him: Tírechán about 670, Muirchú before 700, and Jocelin in the late 1100s'.
Binchy: Britannica calls him 'the most austerely critical of Patrician scholars', not a critic of the legends. Now 'the strictest of modern scholars of Patrick'.

Spelling: 'Banavem Taberniae' in the first moment now matches 'Bannavem Taberniae' in the facts and the page's birthPlace (the Book of Armagh's and Muirchú's spelling; White's translation prints Banavem).
'He signs himself' is 'He calls himself' (the Letter opens 'I confess that I am a bishop, appointed by God, in Ireland'). 'A worthier deathbed' is 'a grander deathbed' (no judgement on the real one).
left_for_owner: The east column's 30 March row (old-calendar churches) is an inference from the OCA's 17 March; no old-calendar church's own calendar was checked, and the Russian Church's 2017 addition is not claimed.
The band (Tiepolo) is 1115 x 1920 and shows a bare-chested sick man at the foot of the painting; the phone and wide crops show only Patrick's upper half, so it stays.
Olden's belief that Martin taught Patrick is now on the page beside Bury's dates: Martin's own page may want the link back (the main session's call).
